old: Its name began as a word for wound cloth worn on the head, long before it meant anything with petals.
The flower was named for a resemblance — its shape reminded people of a wrapped headpiece.
It shares an ancestor with the English word 'turban,' just took a different path through French to get here.
clues: This spring flower takes its name from an old Persian word for a turban, the length of cloth people once wound around their heads.
Grown from a bulb, it holds one cup-shaped bloom on a tall stem, unlike a daffodil's trumpet. The name likely stuck because that bloom recalled a wrapped turban.
Holland is famous for vast, striped fields of these in red, yellow and pink each spring, and an old song invites you to tiptoe through them.
